newsitem.title: ZAIRE: Zaire's copper city awaits rebels, few expect war.
newsitem.headline: Zaire's copper city awaits rebels, few expect war.

text.p: Zaireans in the copper capital Lubumbashi said on Wednesday they want their city to be the next target for rebel leader Laurent Kabila and promised him little resistance when he comes.
So far all has been quiet with only the barking of dogs breaking the silence at night.

Kabila said on Tuesday he may be tempted to head instead for the capital Kinshasa in the west or for the diamond capital of Mbuji-Mayi deeper in the interior, leaving the cities tensely playing a waiting game to see who's next.
"I'd rather he came yesterday," said Jean, a Lubumbashi security guard sitting uncomfortably on a metal frame that was once a chair, a sign of poverty he blamed on ailing President Mobutu Sese Seko.
"Kabila can walk in here, we're waiting for him. Many soldiers were sent to defend Kisangani. They armed it to the teeth, and look where that got them," said Katumba, 30.
"Even those who stayed have been fleeing their barracks and deserting. They've been finding sacks full of abandoned weapons and uniforms. There won't be any resistance here."
Kabila's forces are some 400 km away in the north of Shaba province, known as Katanga by those who want greater autonomy.

After Kabila's forces took heavily defended Kisangani, Zaire's third largest city, at the weekend with barely a fight, he vowed his next target would be Lubumbashi, far away to the south in Shaba which is rich in copper and other minerals.
"We are waiting for liberation. Kabila is one of us, a Katangan," Jean said, adding he hoped a new government would bring a Zairean federation and ultimately independence for the province of Katanga.
Kabila himself is from the province and took part in the earliest of its many attempts to secede after the then Belgian Congo won independence in 1960.
As in Kinshasa, the view of the man in the street in Lubumbashi is the sooner the better for the arrival of Kabila, once comrade in arms of Che Guevara but who now espouses capitalism.
People in the city, some 2,900 km south-east of Kinshasa, feared government soldiers may loot before they flee.
Like many local people, Jean said revenue from Zaire's potentially richest region was creamed off by distant Kinshasa.

However the profits are not great. A series of calamities -- a mine collapse, ethnic expulsions, civil strife, corruption and mismanagement -- have left Shaba's economy in a mess, but recent foreign investors hope they can turn it around.
Kabila says he wants to keep Zaire and its 40 million people from hundreds of ethnic groups together as one nation.
The success of his five-month rebellion, which now covers a fifth of Zaire, has sown panic in the unpopular government.

Parliamentarians have voted to sack Prime Minister Kengo wa Dondo in a resolution that fell short of a binding majority but caused joy in Lubumbashi. Kengo was in Kenya on Wednesday for a regional peace conference that Kabila has scorned.
"Hopefully the rest of them will pack up and go now and give us back our country and leave us in Shaba alone," said one engineer, reluctant to give his name.
He said he was looking forward to ripping down portraits of Mobutu, in his trademark leopard-skin hat, that preside over offices and public halls across Zaire.
